subproblem.title: Finite unions of modular domains give fundamental domains modulo ±I
subproblem.statement: Let Δ be a finite-index subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) containing −I, and let μ be hyperbolic measure dx dy/y² on the upper half-plane. There exists a finite set R ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) such that, with F₀ = {x+iy : y>0, |x|≤1/2, x²+y²≥1} and F = ⋃_{r∈R} rF₀, the set F is measurable and, for μ-almost every z, there exists γ∈Δ with γz∈F such that every δ∈Δ satisfying δz∈F obeys δ=γ or δ=−γ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (Δ : Subgroup (Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ)) [Δ.FiniteIndex], (-1 : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ) ∈ Δ → ∃ R : Finset (Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ), let F : Set UpperHalfPlane := ⋃ r ∈ R, (fun z : UpperHalfPlane => r • z) '' ModularGroup.fd; MeasurableSet F ∧ (∀ᵐ z ∂(MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure UpperHalfPlane), ∃ γ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ, γ ∈ Δ ∧ γ • z ∈ F ∧ ∀ δ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ, δ ∈ Δ → δ • z ∈ F → δ = γ ∨ δ = -γ)
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Put G=SL₂(ℤ). Finite index gives finitely many right cosets Δr. Choose exactly one representative of each and let R be their finite set. Define F=⋃_{r∈R}rF₀, where F₀=ModularGroup.fd. Write F₀°=ModularGroup.fdo.
2. The defining inequalities make F₀ closed relative to the upper half-plane. Every element of G acts by a homeomorphism, so each rF₀ is measurable and their finite union F is measurable. The set E=F₀\F₀° is contained in the two vertical lines x=±1/2 and the circle x²+y²=1. Each has planar measure zero: a line has zero area, and the vertical sections of the circle have at most two points, so Fubini gives zero area. The formula μ=dx dy/y² therefore gives μ(E)=0.
3. Möbius transformations preserve μ. Explicitly, for A=((a,b),(c,d)) with positive determinant, Im(Az)=det(A)Im(z)/|cz+d|² and its real Jacobian is det(A)²/|cz+d|⁴; these factors cancel in dx dy/y². This is also the invariant-measure instance in the pinned UpperHalfPlane/Measure.lean. Thus every translate aE is null. The group G is countable because its matrices have four integer entries, so N=⋃_{a∈G}aE is measurable, null, and G-invariant.
4. For any z, ModularGroup.exists_smul_mem_fd gives g∈G with gz∈F₀. Write g⁻¹=ηr with η∈Δ and r∈R. Then η⁻¹z=r(gz)∈F. Consequently there is γ∈Δ with γz∈F.
5. Fix z outside N and such a γ. Suppose δ∈Δ also has δz∈F. Choose r,s∈R and w,v∈F₀ with γz=rw and δz=sv. Since z is outside the G-invariant set N, neither w nor v belongs to E; in particular w∈F₀°. The matrix a=s⁻¹δγ⁻¹r satisfies aw=v∈F₀. By ModularGroup.eq_one_or_neg_one_of_mem_fdo_mem_fd, a=I or a=−I.
6. It follows that δγ⁻¹=sr⁻¹ or δγ⁻¹=−sr⁻¹. The left side belongs to Δ, and −I∈Δ, so sr⁻¹∈Δ in either case. Hence Δs=Δr. Uniqueness of the chosen coset representatives gives s=r, and then δγ⁻¹=I or −I. Thus δ=γ or δ=−γ.
7. Steps 4–6 establish the required representative property outside the null set N. Together with measurability from step 2, this proves the statement for the finite set R.
proof_key_steps: Choose finite representatives of the right cosets Δr.
Show the standard-domain boundary is hyperbolically null and its countable G-saturation remains null.
Use modular-domain covering to obtain a Δ-translate in the finite union.
Use interior uniqueness modulo ±I and uniqueness of coset representatives to prove the required almost-everywhere uniqueness.

subproblem.title: A domain-independent Petersson core for finite-index subgroups
subproblem.statement: Let Δ be a finite-index subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) containing −I, regarded in GL₂(ℝ) by the canonical embedding. Put V=CuspForm Δ 2, μ=dx dy/y², and P(f,g)(z)=conjugate(f(z))g(z)(Im z)². There exists B : InnerProductSpace.Core ℂ V such that the following holds for every measurable F⊂ℍ: if for μ-almost every z there is γ∈Δ with γz∈F and every δ∈Δ with δz∈F satisfies δ=γ or δ=−γ, then, for every f,g∈V, P(f,g) is integrable on F and B.inner f g=∫_F P(f,g)dμ. The same B works for every such F.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (Δ : Subgroup (Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ)) [Δ.FiniteIndex], (-1 : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ) ∈ Δ → ∃ B : InnerProductSpace.Core ℂ (CuspForm Δ 2), ∀ (F : Set UpperHalfPlane), MeasurableSet F → (∀ᵐ z ∂(MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure UpperHalfPlane), ∃ γ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ, γ ∈ Δ ∧ γ • z ∈ F ∧ ∀ δ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ, δ ∈ Δ → δ • z ∈ F → δ = γ ∨ δ = -γ) → ∀ f g : CuspForm Δ 2, MeasureTheory.IntegrableOn (UpperHalfPlane.petersson 2 f g) F (MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure UpperHalfPlane) ∧ B.inner f g = MeasureTheory.integral ((MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure UpperHalfPlane).restrict F) (UpperHalfPlane.petersson 2 f g)
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Fix Δ as in the statement. Apply effective_domain to obtain a finite set R and a measurable domain E=⋃_{r∈R}rF₀ satisfying its almost-everywhere representative property. All integrations below use the canonical hyperbolic measure μ, without an index normalization.
2. For every σ∈SL₂(ℤ), the conjugate σ⁻¹Δσ has finite index. Among sufficiently many nonnegative powers of T=((1,1),(0,1)), two belong to the same right coset of this subgroup. Taking their quotient gives T^h∈σ⁻¹Δσ for some integer h>0. Thus σ∞ is a cusp of Δ, and, for any f∈V, f|₂σ is h-periodic and tends to zero as the imaginary part tends to infinity. Every rational boundary point, including infinity, has the form σ∞: a primitive integer pair representing it can be completed to a determinant-one matrix by Bézout's identity.
3. Fix r∈R and write u=f|₂r. It is holomorphic, has a positive period h as above, and tends to zero at infinity. The map q=exp(2πiz/h) identifies the quotient by this period with the punctured unit disk. Periodicity makes u descend to a holomorphic function there. Its zero limit supplies boundedness near zero, so the removable-singularity theorem extends it holomorphically with value zero. Write the extension as qU(q), where U is holomorphic. On any smaller closed disk U is bounded. Consequently there are C,Y with |u(x+iy)|≤C exp(−2πy/h) for all y≥Y, uniformly in x. Applying the same reasoning to v=g|₂r gives a common threshold and an exponentially decaying bound for |uv|. This is the cusp-decay argument formalized in the pinned QExpansion.lean.
4. The weight-two slash formula is (f|₂A)(z)=det(A)(cz+d)⁻²f(Az) for positive-determinant A. Substituting Im(Az)=det(A)Im(z)/|cz+d|² gives P(f|₂A,g|₂A)(z)=P(f,g)(Az). Together with preservation of μ, this shows that the integral of |P(f,g)| on rF₀ equals the planar integral of |(f|₂r)(z)(g|₂r)(z)| on F₀. The high part is bounded by C′exp(−ay), with a>0 and horizontal width at most one, so its integral is finite. Choose the height threshold at least one. The remaining part of F₀ is contained in the compact set |x|≤1/2 and √3/2≤y≤Y; continuity bounds the integrand there. Hence P(f,g) is integrable on each rF₀ and therefore on E. Its measurability follows from continuity.
5. Slash invariance of f and g and the covariance identity imply that P(f,g) is Δ-invariant. Now let F be any measurable set satisfying the representative hypothesis. The exceptional sets for the representative properties of E and F are measurable and null: their predicates involve only countably many measurable translates. Remove their countable Δ-saturations. The remaining set X is measurable, conull, and Δ-invariant, and both representative properties hold at every point of X.
6. Choose a countable set L of representatives of Δ/{±I}. The sets E∩X∩γF, for γ∈L, partition E∩X. Coverage follows from the representative property of F, and disjointness follows from uniqueness modulo ±I. Translating each piece by γ⁻¹ gives F∩X∩γ⁻¹E; these partition F∩X by the property of E. Invariance of μ and P first gives equality of the nonnegative absolute integrals on the two partitions. Thus ∫_F|P(f,g)|dμ=∫_E|P(f,g)|dμ<∞. Countable additivity for the now absolutely integrable complex function gives ∫_F P(f,g)dμ=∫_E P(f,g)dμ.
7. Define B(f,g)=∫_E P(f,g)dμ. Step 4 ensures integrability for every pair, including sums and scalar multiples. The pointwise identities P(f₁+f₂,g)=P(f₁,g)+P(f₂,g), P(cf,g)=conjugate(c)P(f,g), and P(g,f)=conjugate(P(f,g)) therefore pass through the integral. They give additivity, conjugate-linearity in the first variable, and conjugate symmetry. In particular, B is linear in the second variable.
8. The diagonal integrand P(f,f)(z)=|f(z)|²(Im z)² is real and nonnegative. Its integral has nonnegative real part. If B(f,f)=0, the integral of this nonnegative real function is zero, so it vanishes μ-almost everywhere on E. Its Δ-invariance and countability of Δ extend this vanishing to almost every point of ⋃_{γ∈Δ}γE. The representative property of E makes this union conull, so the diagonal integrand vanishes almost everywhere on ℍ.
9. If f(z₀) were nonzero, continuity would give an open disk U about z₀, with closure inside ℍ, and ε>0 such that |f(z)|²(Im z)²≥ε on U. The imaginary coordinate is bounded above on U, so the density y⁻² has a strictly positive lower bound there. Since an open disk has positive planar area, μ(U)>0. This contradicts the almost-everywhere vanishing. Therefore f vanishes pointwise, and extensionality gives f=0 in V.
10. Steps 7–9 supply exactly the conjugate symmetry, nonnegative real diagonal, additivity, conjugate scalar law, and definiteness fields of InnerProductSpace.Core. Construct B with inner product given by the integral over E. For every admissible F, step 6 supplies both the stated integrability and the identity B.inner f g=∫_F P(f,g)dμ. Since E and B were fixed before F, one Core works for all such domains.
proof_key_steps: Obtain a finite union of modular-domain translates from effective_domain.
Use finite-index cusp widths and the punctured-disk coordinate to establish uniform exponential cusp decay.
Combine Petersson covariance with cusp decay and compactness to prove absolute integrability.
Partition two domains using Δ/{±I} to prove integrability transfer and domain independence.
Pass the sesquilinear and conjugate-symmetry identities through the integral.
Use nonnegativity, almost-everywhere coverage, continuity, and positive measure of open disks to prove definiteness.
Construct one Core representing the integral on every admissible domain.

subproblem.title: Good-prime Hecke adjointness for the unnormalized Petersson integral
subproblem.statement: Let M be a nonzero natural number and Γ=Γ₀(M). Let μ=dx dy/y² and P(f,g)(z)=conjugate(f(z))g(z)(Im z)². Suppose F⊂ℍ is measurable and, for μ-almost every z, there exists γ∈Γ with γz∈F such that every δ∈Γ satisfying δz∈F obeys δ=γ or δ=−γ. For every natural prime p not dividing M, every witnesses hp and hpM, and every f,g∈CuspForm Γ 2, the exact operator T=CuspForm.heckeTLin 2 hp hpM satisfies ∫_F P(Tf,g)dμ=∫_F P(f,Tg)dμ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (M : ℕ) [NeZero M] (F : Set UpperHalfPlane), MeasurableSet F → (∀ᵐ z ∂(MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure UpperHalfPlane), ∃ γ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ, γ ∈ (CongruenceSubgroup.Gamma0 M) ∧ γ • z ∈ F ∧ ∀ δ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ, δ ∈ (CongruenceSubgroup.Gamma0 M) → δ • z ∈ F → δ = γ ∨ δ = -γ) → ∀ (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (hpM : ¬ p ∣ M) (f g : CuspForm (CongruenceSubgroup.Gamma0 M) 2), MeasureTheory.integral ((MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure UpperHalfPlane).restrict F) (UpperHalfPlane.petersson 2 (CuspForm.heckeTLin 2 hp hpM f) g) = MeasureTheory.integral ((MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure UpperHalfPlane).restrict F) (UpperHalfPlane.petersson 2 f (CuspForm.heckeTLin 2 hp hpM g))
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Fix M,F,p,hp,hpM,f,g as in the statement, and write Γ=Γ₀(M). The principal subgroup Γ(M), the kernel of reduction modulo M, has finite index because the reduction group is finite. It is contained in Γ, so Γ has finite index. Also −I∈Γ. Thus petersson_integral_core applies to Γ. Since p is prime, p>0; since p does not divide M, gcd(p,M)=1.
2. For a positive-determinant real matrix A=((a,b),(c,d)), use the frozen formula (u|₂A)(z)=det(A)(cz+d)⁻²u(Az). Multiplication of denominators and determinants proves (u|₂A)|₂B=u|₂(AB). A positive scalar matrix tI acts trivially because its determinant t² cancels its denominator factor t². The imaginary-part formula gives P(u|₂A,v|₂A)(z)=P(u,v)(Az), and the real Jacobian gives preservation of μ. These are the weight-two specialization of UpperHalfPlane.petersson_slash and the pinned hyperbolic-measure invariance result.
3. Put α=diag(1,p), H=Γ∩α⁻¹Γα, and K=Γ∩αΓα⁻¹, with intersections taken after embedding the matrices in GL₂(ℚ). For γ=((a,b),(c,d))∈Γ, conjugation gives αγα⁻¹=((a,b/p),(pc,d)), so γ∈H exactly when p divides b. Likewise α⁻¹γα=((a,pb),(c/p,d)), so γ∈K exactly when pM divides c. Both subgroups contain Γ(pM), hence have finite index in SL₂(ℤ), and both contain −I. Directly from their definitions, αHα⁻¹=K.
4. The required slash translates are cusp forms on these subgroups. For any finite-index subgroup Δ of SL₂(ℤ), the coset argument with powers of T gives a positive cusp width at each rational point σ∞. Conversely, a noncentral integer parabolic has either infinity as fixed point or the repeated root (a−d)/(2c) of cz²+(d−a)z−b=0; hence every cusp is rational. Thus Γ,H,K have exactly the rational cusps. If A is a positive-determinant rational matrix and L=Γ∩A⁻¹ΓA has finite index, then f|₂A is L-invariant: AhA⁻¹∈Γ implies (f|₂A)|₂h=f|₂A. It is holomorphic by the slash formula. At a rational cusp σ∞ choose ρ∈SL₂(ℤ) carrying infinity to Aσ∞. Then ρ⁻¹Aσ=((a,b),(0,d)) with a/d>0, and ((f|₂A)|₂σ)(z)=(a/d)(f|₂ρ)((a/d)z+b/d), which tends to zero at infinity. The single-coordinate criterion OnePoint.isZeroAt_iff makes this the full bundled cusp condition. Restriction from Γ to H or K also preserves cusp forms because the cusp sets coincide. Apply this argument to A=α and A=α⁻¹: f|₂α and g are cusp forms on H, while f and g|₂α⁻¹ are cusp forms on K.
5. Compute the right cosets H\Γ. For γ₁,γ₂∈Γ, the upper-right entry of γ₁γ₂⁻¹ is b₁a₂−a₁b₂. Thus Hγ₁=Hγ₂ exactly when their first rows modulo p are proportional. These rows are nonzero because their determinants are one, and ℤ/pℤ is a field. The projective lines with first coordinate nonzero are represented uniquely by (1,j), 0≤j<p; choose t_j=((1,j),(0,1))∈Γ. Bézout gives integers u,v with pu+Mv=1. Set γ*=((p,−v),(M,u)) and β=((1,−v),(M,pu)). Both have determinant one and lower-left entry M, so belong to Γ. Modulo p, the first row of γ* is (0,−v), with v nonzero because Mv=1 modulo p. It therefore represents the remaining projective line. The matrices t_j and γ* form a complete nonrepeating set of right-coset representatives.
6. The assignment Hγ↦Γαγ identifies H\Γ with the left-Γ cosets in ΓαΓ: equality of Γαγ₁ and Γαγ₂ is equivalent to γ₁γ₂⁻¹∈Γ∩α⁻¹Γα. Define A_j=((1,j),(0,p)) and C=diag(p,1). Since αt_j=A_j and αγ*=βC, the double coset is the disjoint union of the left cosets ΓA_j and ΓC. In particular C∈ΓαΓ, so ΓCΓ=ΓαΓ. Since α⁻¹=p⁻¹C and scalar matrices are central, Γα⁻¹Γ=p⁻¹ΓαΓ; its left cosets have representatives p⁻¹A_j and p⁻¹C.
7. For a Γ-invariant function u, let D_αu be the slash sum over left-coset representatives in ΓαΓ. Changing a representative by left multiplication by Γ leaves its summand unchanged, by slash composition and Γ-invariance. Step 6 and the pinned definitions give D_αu=Σ_{0≤j<p}u|₂A_j+u|₂C=ModularForm.heckeT 2 p u. Positive scalars act trivially by step 2, so the inverse double-coset sum D_{α⁻¹}u is the same function. For cusp forms, the coe_heckeTLin_apply identity identifies both sums with the underlying function of the exact bundled operator T=CuspForm.heckeTLin 2 hp hpM.
8. Choose right-coset representatives γ_i for H\Γ and δ_j for K\Γ. Put E_H=⋃_iγ_iF and E_K=⋃_jδ_jF. These are finite measurable unions. To handle all exceptional sets simultaneously, remove the saturation of the null exceptional set for F under the countable group generated by Γ and α. Every element of this group preserves μ, so its complement X is conull and invariant. For z∈X, choose η∈Γ with ηz∈F and write η⁻¹=hγ_i; then h⁻¹z∈γ_iF. This proves H-coverage. If h₁z∈γ_iF and h₂z∈γ_jF, uniqueness for F gives γ_j⁻¹h₂h₁⁻¹γ_i=±I. Since −I∈H, the representative cosets agree, so i=j and h₂=±h₁. Thus E_H satisfies the effective fundamental-domain condition for H. The identical argument with K and δ_j proves it for E_K. It also shows that their displayed pieces are pairwise disjoint outside null sets.
9. By petersson_integral_core applied to H, the function P(f|₂α,g) is integrable on E_H. Restricting to each piece and transporting it to F proves integrability of every summand P(f|₂αγ_i,g) on F. Consequently finite-sum linearity, Γ-invariance of g, and covariance give ∫_F P(D_αf,g)dμ=Σ_i∫_F P(f|₂αγ_i,g)dμ=Σ_i∫_{γ_iF}P(f|₂α,g)dμ=∫_{E_H}P(f|₂α,g)dμ.
10. Slash composition gives g=(g|₂α⁻¹)|₂α. Covariance therefore rewrites the last integrand as P(f,g|₂α⁻¹)(αz). The measure-preserving substitution w=αz yields ∫_{E_H}P(f|₂α,g)dμ=∫_{αE_H}P(f,g|₂α⁻¹)dμ.
11. Conjugation αHα⁻¹=K shows that αE_H satisfies the effective fundamental-domain property for K: transport the representative in H by α, and transport uniqueness by the same conjugation; ±I are unchanged. The image is measurable because α acts by a homeomorphism, and null exceptional sets remain null. By step 4, f and g|₂α⁻¹ are cusp forms on K. Apply the single Core supplied by petersson_integral_core for K to the domains αE_H and E_K. Its two integral identities prove ∫_{αE_H}P(f,g|₂α⁻¹)dμ=∫_{E_K}P(f,g|₂α⁻¹)dμ, and also give absolute integrability on both domains.
12. Split the last integral over the almost-everywhere disjoint pieces δ_jF and transport each piece to F. Since f|₂δ_j=f, covariance gives ∫_{E_K}P(f,g|₂α⁻¹)dμ=Σ_j∫_F P(f,g|₂α⁻¹δ_j)dμ=∫_F P(f,D_{α⁻¹}g)dμ. All summands are integrable by restriction of the integral on E_K and change of variables. The matrices α⁻¹δ_j represent the inverse double coset because its coset correspondence uses Γ∩αΓα⁻¹=K.
13. Combining steps 9–12 proves ∫_F P(D_αf,g)dμ=∫_F P(f,D_{α⁻¹}g)dμ. Substitute the two exact identifications with T from step 7. This is the required equality. Every pairing used the unnormalized integral and each coset occurred once, so no index factor is introduced. The underlying-function identity for heckeTLin holds for every hp and hpM; hence the conclusion has exactly the stated quantification over proof witnesses.
